question: Can a learned, permutation-equivariant policy greedily select and place unordered textureless polygon fragments so that they reconstruct a supplied two-dimensional target shape, including cases with different fragment counts, rotations, and damaged or missing pieces?

key_findings.claim: Fragment Assembly Network decomposes each greedy assembly step into set-conditioned fragment selection and dense pose prediction.
key_findings.evidence: FAN-Select scores every candidate using the candidate, remaining target region, and all other fragments; FAN-Pose predicts a pixel probability map and an optional distribution over discrete rotation bins. Fragment Relation Attention Modules apply multi-head attention to candidate sets, so parameter count does not depend on fragment count and permuting inputs permutes the corresponding outputs.

anchors.section: 3. Geometric Shape Assembly and 3.1 Fragment Assembly Networks
Fragment Relation Attention Modules and 3.2 Training

key_findings.claim: On eight-piece synthetic square, pentagon, and hexagon tasks, FAN covers more of the target with much higher near-complete reconstruction rates than the optimization baselines while running in under a second per instance.
key_findings.evidence: For square, FAN obtains Cov@0.95 0.470, Cov@0.90 0.649, mean coverage 0.914, and IoU 0.882 in under one second. Simulated annealing and Bayesian optimization obtain zero Cov@0.95/Cov@0.90, coverage 0.720/0.730, IoU 0.655/0.664, and 1,860/155 seconds. FAN obtains coverage 0.922 and IoU 0.884 on pentagon and 0.916/0.882 on hexagon, again with nonzero high-threshold success where both optimizers have zero.

key_findings.claim: FAN also outperforms the tested baselines on axis-aligned Mondrian-square partitions, where many rectangular fragments are mutually ambiguous.
key_findings.evidence: FAN reaches Cov@0.95 0.384, Cov@0.90 0.545, mean coverage 0.892, and IoU 0.854. Simulated annealing and Bayesian optimization have zero near-complete reconstructions and coverage/IoU of 0.761/0.671 and 0.756/0.704; the modified LayoutGAN reaches 0.549/0.545. FAN and LayoutGAN run in under one second, while the optimization methods take 153 and 97 seconds.

key_findings.claim: The task becomes sharply harder as fragment count and rotation resolution increase, despite the architecture accepting variable-size sets.
key_findings.evidence: With four fragments, mean coverage is 0.991 and Cov@0.95 is 0.940-0.972 across the three target shapes. With sixteen fragments, mean coverage falls to 0.769-0.797 and Cov@0.95 to 0.008-0.024. With four rotation bins, mean coverage ranges from 0.670 to 0.791; with twenty bins it drops to 0.603-0.640, and Cov@0.90 and Cov@0.95 are zero for every target.

key_findings.claim: Set attention helps, but the training assembly order is a much larger determinant of success than the aggregation module alone.
key_findings.evidence: Replacing FRAM with average pooling reduces square Cov@0.95 from 0.470 to 0.431 and mean coverage from 0.914 to 0.899. Replacing the bottom-left-to-top-right sequence rule with the paper's random adjacency-based sampling reduces square Cov@0.95 from 0.470 to 0.012 and coverage from 0.914 to 0.814; similarly large drops occur for pentagon and hexagon. The supplementary material states that consistent supervised sequences are crucial.

anchors.section: Effectiveness of FRAM and Sequence Sampling Strategy

key_findings.claim: FAN retains partial coverage under missing, eroded, and distorted fragments, but the abnormal-fragment experiment does not establish superiority over another method.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 reports FAN mean coverage/IoU of 0.808/0.716 for a missing square fragment, 0.843/0.803 for eroded square fragments, and 0.753/0.685 for distorted square fragments, with comparable results on pentagon and hexagon. The text says the method outperforms others, but Table 4 contains no baseline rows and scores exclude degradation from the ground-truth target, so it supports robustness only in an absolute sense.

key_findings.claim: The paper demonstrates learned reconstruction within a synthetic 2D raster world, not a general physical assembly system.
key_findings.evidence: Training and evaluation use 5,000 procedurally binary-partitioned samples per target, exact fragment masks, an exact target mask, 128×128 CNN inputs, discrete rotations, and supervised assembly sequences. The texture result is qualitative, and there is no camera input, depth, occlusion, grasping, collision, tolerance, dynamics, or real-fragment evaluation.

method.core_idea: Learn a greedy inverse of procedural fragmentation: at each step, relate all remaining pieces to the unfilled target, choose one piece, and predict its translation and discretized rotation.
method.mechanism: Binary space partitioning turns a target mask into 2^K polygon fragments, assigns a consistent bottom-left-to-top-right supervised sequence, and randomly rotates the pieces. FAN encodes each candidate, other candidates, and the remaining target region. A transformer-like Fragment Relation Attention Module aggregates high-order relations without depending on set cardinality. FAN-Select uses cross-entropy to choose the next piece; FAN-Pose uses an encoder-decoder to output a 128×128 placement map and rotation-bin probabilities, trained with multiscale pooled position losses. At inference the highest-scoring fragment and pose are committed greedily and removed until no candidate remains.
assumptions: An exact target silhouette and clean segmentation masks for every fragment are available before assembly.
Subtracting the current binary assembly from the target produces a meaningful remaining-shape input even after earlier overlaps or pose errors.
Procedural binary partitions of squares, pentagons, and hexagons capture the geometric ambiguity of downstream fragment assembly.
A fixed bottom-left-to-top-right teacher sequence is learnable and remains appropriate when shapes, counts, and damage patterns change.
Greedy local selection and placement are sufficient without backtracking, beam search, or global pose refinement.
A finite rotation-bin set approximates required orientations closely enough for the coverage metric.
Cardinality-independent parameters confer useful variable-count generalization, even though the count studies use newly prepared datasets.
Raster resolution and the center-position representation retain the mating geometry needed to place arbitrary polygons.

techniques.role: Creates supervised inverse-assembly episodes by recursively splitting a target polygon and hiding original poses.
Models relations among a variable-size unordered candidate set while preserving one output score per fragment.
Reduces combinatorial assembly to repeated classification of the next fragment.
Predicts a spatial distribution over fragment-center locations rather than regressing one coordinate directly.
Represents orientation as one of a fixed number of angle bins.
Supervises pooled versions of the target location map to provide gradients at several spatial scales.
Uses a bottom-left-to-top-right ordering so otherwise equivalent assembly trajectories produce consistent labels.

evaluations.setting: Eight-fragment Square, Pentagon, and Hexagon datasets, 5,000 procedural samples per shape with 64/16/20% train/validation/test splits
evaluations.metric: Cov@0.95, Cov@0.90, mean coverage, IoU, and runtime
evaluations.result: FAN obtains coverage 0.914/0.922/0.916 and IoU 0.882/0.884/0.882, with Cov@0.95 0.470/0.452/0.439 and runtime under one second.
evaluations.baseline: Simulated annealing and Bayesian optimization, both with zero Cov@0.90 and runtimes of 149-1,860 seconds; modified LayoutGAN on Square only

evaluations.result: FAN reaches 0.384, 0.545, 0.892, and 0.854 respectively in under one second.
evaluations.baseline: Simulated annealing (coverage 0.761, IoU 0.671), Bayesian optimization (0.756, 0.704), and modified LayoutGAN (0.549, 0.545)

evaluations.result: FRAM reaches 0.470/0.649/0.914/0.882; average pooling reaches 0.431/0.580/0.899/0.863 and no aggregation 0.392/0.569/0.899/0.863.

evaluations.metric: Cov@0.95, Cov@0.90, mean coverage, and IoU

limitations: All quantitative tests are synthetic 2D raster puzzles built from simple square, pentagon, hexagon, or axis-aligned square targets; there is no real fragment, archaeological, manufacturing, or robotic assembly evaluation.
The model receives an exact target mask and exact candidate-fragment masks, bypassing perception, segmentation, pose uncertainty, occlusion, and correspondence extraction.

The variable-count experiment prepares datasets for each count, so it demonstrates architectural compatibility and in-distribution performance at four or sixteen pieces, not clearly zero-shot count generalization from the eight-piece model.
Performance collapses as combinatorics increase: sixteen pieces rarely exceed 0.95 coverage, and twenty rotation bins produce no examples above 0.90 coverage.
The greedy policy has no backtracking, global collision constraint, remaining-parts feasibility check, or final joint pose refinement, so early mistakes propagate.

Training depends heavily on a handcrafted bottom-left-to-top-right order; the random-order ablation loses most near-complete assemblies, showing that sequence supervision encodes substantial solution structure.

The main baselines are weak matches: simulated annealing and Bayesian optimization use local IoU objectives, while the modified LayoutGAN cannot handle variable polygon vertex counts and is unavailable for Pentagon and Hexagon.
The abnormal-fragment text claims outperformance, but Table 4 reports only FAN and evaluates after excluding degradation from the target, preventing a direct comparative robustness conclusion.
Texture handling is demonstrated only qualitatively on selected ImageNet examples, with no split, aggregate metric, or comparison.
Rotation is discretized rather than estimated continuously, and accuracy worsens sharply at finer discretization.
The experiments report point estimates without seeds, uncertainty intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity to fragmentation randomness.
No physical feasibility is modeled: pieces can overlap, exact placement tolerances are absent, and there is no grasping, collision, stability, force, or execution noise.
failure_modes: Repeated or symmetric fragments yield nearly interchangeable selection and pose labels, especially for axis-aligned partitions.
A wrong early placement corrupts the computed remaining-shape mask and can cause cascading selection and overlap errors.
Many small fragments expand the decision horizon and reduce near-complete reconstruction probability even when average coverage remains moderate.
Fine rotation bins make orientation classification brittle, while coarse bins introduce unavoidable geometric misalignment.
An assembly requiring an order unlike the canonical bottom-left sweep can fall outside the learned trajectory distribution.
Missing or distorted pieces make exact target completion impossible and can prompt the greedy policy to place incompatible fragments into residual gaps.
Thin, highly concave, curved, or subpixel mating boundaries may be lost in 128×128 raster features and pooled pose supervision.
Novel partition generators, target topology, fragment-count regimes, or real sensor masks may break the learned procedural prior.
Ignoring physical constraints can turn a high-IoU image solution into an unreachable or unstable robot plan.
reusable_insights: Represent unordered parts with permutation-equivariant attention, but evaluate count generalization with a model trained on disjoint counts rather than merely changing set size.
Decomposing assembly into piece selection and dense pose prediction is efficient, yet a global refinement or search stage is needed to repair greedy errors.
Canonicalizing interchangeable action sequences can make supervised learning tractable, but order robustness must be measured because the canonicalizer may carry much of the solution.
Report both mean overlap and stringent completion thresholds; high average coverage can conceal almost total failure at exact assembly.
Rotation resolution is a core difficulty axis and should be paired with continuous-angle refinement rather than only increasing class count.
Procedural fragmentation supplies unlimited supervision, but transfer claims require held-out generators, target families, and real masks.
Robustness to damaged pieces needs an explicit achievable-target definition, a coverage/abstention policy, and matched competing methods.
Relational attention can improve near-complete assembly more than it changes average overlap, so tail-quality metrics reveal its main benefit.
open_questions: Can a model trained only on eight fragments generalize zero-shot to unseen counts and much longer horizons?
Would beam search, backtracking, or differentiable global pose refinement recover the large gap between mean coverage and near-complete assembly?
Can continuous SE(2)-equivariant pose prediction replace brittle rotation bins while preserving permutation equivariance?
How much performance survives held-out target topologies, curved fragments, non-binary fracture processes, and real segmentation noise?
Can training marginalize over all valid assembly orders rather than imposing a bottom-left teacher trajectory?
How should the system detect missing, extra, or incompatible pieces and abstain from impossible completion?
What is the right matched-search baseline when every candidate placement can be scored against the exact target silhouette?
Can an image-space solver be coupled to collision-aware robotic planning and maintain its advantage under grasp and execution uncertainty?
Which ambiguity measure over remaining pieces predicts when greedy selection is unsafe and search should be invoked?

competitive_landscape.title: Form2Fit: Learning Shape Priors for Generalizable Assembly from Disassembly
competitive_landscape.difference: Form2Fit learns surface descriptors and object-to-kit correspondences from real robotic disassembly, then executes pick-and-place on novel kits. FAN instead solves a supplied 2D target silhouette from arbitrary polygon fragments by sequential selection and dense pose prediction; it addresses stronger combinatorics in image space but omits perception and physical execution.

competitive_landscape.title: Learn2Assemble with Structured Representations and Search for Robotic Architectural Construction
competitive_landscape.difference: Learn2Assemble combines a multi-head attention graph, model-free reinforcement learning, Monte Carlo planning, and robot-in-the-loop feasibility for stable 3D structures made from building blocks. FAN uses supervised inverse-fragmentation and greedy 2D pose maps for non-unit polygon pieces; it is faster and simpler but has no search, stability, or execution layer.

competitive_landscape.title: PuzzleFusion: Unleashing the Power of Diffusion Models for Spatial Puzzle Solving
competitive_landscape.difference: PuzzleFusion generates all piece translations and rotations through iterative diffusion and evaluates synthetic Voronoi jigsaws plus real MagicPlan room layouts. FAN commits one selected fragment at a time and conditions on an explicit target mask; its key advantages are a lightweight greedy decomposition and damaged-piece studies, while diffusion offers joint multimodal pose reasoning without a handcrafted sequence.

competitive_landscape.title: DiffAssemble: A Unified Graph-Diffusion Model for 2D and 3D Reassembly
competitive_landscape.difference: DiffAssemble treats pieces as spatial-graph nodes and jointly denoises their positions and rotations across both 2D visual puzzles and 3D fractured objects, reporting state-of-the-art results and an 11× speedup over its quickest optimization baseline. FAN is restricted to sequential 2D raster placement but uniquely studies exact target masks, variable counts, abnormal fragments, and the role of supervised order.

competitive_landscape.title: Rearrangement Planning for General Part Assembly
competitive_landscape.difference: GPAT directly predicts precise poses for unseen 3D parts by matching each part to a novel target and validates on CAD models and real scans. FAN handles unordered synthetic 2D fragments with a selection-plus-placement policy, but its evidence for unseen targets, real geometry, and physical pose generalization is much narrower.

competitive_landscape.title: 3D Geometric Shape Assembly via Efficient Point Cloud Matching
competitive_landscape.difference: PMTR uses coarse- and fine-level local point-cloud correspondences plus an approximate high-order Proxy Match Transform on the large-scale Breaking Bad 3D benchmark. FAN uses global raster/set context and a supplied 2D target rather than mating-surface correspondence; PMTR shows how the geometric-assembly agenda moved toward realistic 3D fragments and scalable matching.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper introduces the challenging learning problem of assembling arbitrary textureless 2D fragments with indistinct junctions and proposes an efficient network that selects and poses pieces while generalizing to variable fragment counts and several abnormal scenarios.
novelty_assessment.evidence: FAN combines set-conditioned fragment selection, dense pose and discrete-angle prediction, and permutation-equivariant relation attention. On the paper's procedural targets it decisively improves coverage, high-threshold completion, and runtime over simulated annealing, Bayesian optimization, and a modified LayoutGAN, and it includes count, damage, rotation, aggregation, and sequence-order studies.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a clean synthetic benchmark for target-conditioned textureless 2D fragment assembly and a fast supervised selection-plus-pose baseline with a useful order-dependence audit. Earlier geometry-based robotic assembly and contemporary attention/search construction already learned relational assembly, so learning for assembly is not new. Later PuzzleFusion, DiffAssemble, GPAT, and PMTR replace the narrow raster/greedy setting with joint diffusion, unseen 3D targets, real scans, or point-cloud correspondence. FAN remains historically useful, but its claims should not be read as zero-shot count generalization, comparative robustness to damaged pieces, or a physical assembly solution.

reviewer_notes: Read all 11 pages of the current locally indexed arXiv v2 text, including the supplementary algorithms, baseline definitions, architecture tables, and every quantitative table. Page anchors use physical PDF pages. Six primary-source competitors were checked at current arXiv or official PMLR records on 2026-08-23. The review preserves the strong synthetic results while explicitly separating cardinality-compatible architecture from zero-shot count transfer, absolute abnormal-piece scores from comparative superiority, and image-space reconstruction from robotic assembly.
